newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-FIFA STILL HOPE TO PERSUADE FRANCE TO TAKE DOWN FENCES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FIFA STILL HOPE TO PERSUADE FRANCE TO TAKE DOWN FENCES.

text.p: World soccer chiefs said on Saturday they still hoped to persuade France to take down perimeter fences for next year's World Cup finals because they created a bad image for the game and the country.

"I will be very sad if there are fences there. The public don't deserve that," said Joao Havelange, the president of world governing body FIFA. "People are not animals to be put in a cage. The public want to see the match."

The success of last year's largely trouble-free European championship in England, where there were no fences, has boosted the argument in favour of taking down the cages. But the French government, which is responsible for security at the finals, is against it.

FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter said the international body had not given up its campaign to persuade the French to change their minds and had already talked to several local councils who were responsible for stadiums.

"We have not given up on this one year before the tournament," Blatter said. "These fences are not a good image for France. We can understand situations where fences may be required behind the goals but we are not sure they are needed along the whole of the side of the pitch."

"We have already talked to local mayors about this. The situation at Montpellier shocked us...They say there is no time...It is a question of image and security. And also a question of spectators not being treated like prisoners."
Blatter said that, like England, Germany had recently shown that it was possible to take down part of the fencing along the pitch without security being affected.
Michel Platini, the joint chief organiser of the 1998 tournament, met FIFA officials on Friday and hinted that there may be a way of finding a flexible solution.
"It is a matter for the state," Platini said. "But the most important thing is stopping the crowd from getting on the pitch. Maybe we can come up with something."
Some French grounds have a moat around the pitch which could be an alternative to fences.
FIFA plans to follow closely an international tournament in France, starting on Tuesday, when matches will be played in some of the World Cup stadiums.
